title: Roses
hook: a dying nun makes a promise about what she'll do after she's gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse in the dark, seated beside those who can't believe. Your line was the table of sinners. When doubt came up, did you listen before you answered? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

A will usually tells other people what to do: who gets the house, which song to play. In the infirmary at Lisieux, Thérèse's sisters wrote down things she said in her last weeks, and one of them is a plan for herself. Not rest. Work. She said she wanted to spend her heaven doing good on earth. And tradition adds an image to go with it: she would let fall a shower of roses. Today, roses.
screen: `A LAST WISH, BUT FOR HERSELF.` → `NOT REST. WORK.` → `A SHOWER OF ROSES.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Her sisters kept notebooks by her bed, and these sayings were later gathered as her last conversations. In them she says that her mission is about to begin, and that she wants to spend her heaven doing good on earth. A strange thing for a dying nun to say: heaven, for her, sounds busy. Second, why Catholics hear it as more than a nice wish. The Church teaches the communion of saints: those who have died in Christ are not cut off from the living, and they pray for us. The Catechism, explaining this, quotes Thérèse's own line about spending her heaven doing good on earth. Her wish became a way the Church explains what saints do. Third, the roses. Tradition says she spoke of letting fall a shower of roses, and people who pray to her tell stories of a rose turning up, a scent, a small unexpected kindness, which they take as her answer. The Church doesn't ask anyone to read signs in flowers. Some people find comfort in the custom; others pass it by. Both are at home in the Church. Fourth, the quiet part. A rose falling doesn't announce who dropped it. The good Thérèse promised is the same kind she did inside the convent walls: small, hidden, unsigned. Jesus puts it this way in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Heaven doing good, and earth doing it too, without a name card.
screen: `SHE PLANS TO WORK IN HEAVEN.` · `THE SAINTS PRAY FOR THE LIVING.` · `A SHOWER OF ROSES.` · then, large: `LET NOT THY LEFT HAND KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one good thing nobody will trace back to you. Settle, and breathe. Look over the people you'll cross today. Who could use something small? A coffee paid for. A dish washed before anyone asks. A kind word passed along about someone, behind their back for once. Choose one, and choose how to keep your name off it. Let it be a rose with no card. If you pray, you can ask Thérèse to pray with you, as Catholics do. If you don't, just hold the plan steady. The bell holds the time.
Roses. Tradition's image for Thérèse's promise to spend her heaven doing good on earth: small kindnesses falling, unsigned. Today's word.
Your line: heaven doing good. Today, do your one good thing quietly, and if someone asks who did it, just smile. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics ask the saints, Thérèse among them, to pray for them, and some keep a custom of asking her for a sign of roses; others simply try to do hidden good in her spirit.
